rashi:a1.1: What are the circumstances? Where they said twenty-one: so that principal and fifth together come to twenty-six and a dinar; and this one adds five [the fifth, to the other man’s twenty-six], which is thirty-one and a dinar.
rashi:a1.2: The owner takes precedence: for if we gave it to this other man, the Temple would lose a dinar compared with what [the owner] offered first. Therefore we go back to the owner, even against his will.
rashi:a1.3: And if not, he says to this one: It has come to you: for the owner says: A man has come in my place [literally, into our breach].
gershom:a1.1: And if not, he says to him: to this one: You give twenty-six shekels, and it has come to you.
rashi:a2.1: Mishna. Of his flock: some of his flock. He says, “These are ḥerem,” and gives them to the priest.
rashi:a2.2: All of them: so that he left nothing for himself.
rashi:a2.3: That a person should spare his property: so as not to squander it on ordinary people.
gershom:a2.1: A person may dedicate some of his flock and his cattle etc.: for the sake of Heaven, in that he can say, “These are ḥerem for me,” and they take effect.
gershom:a3.1: All the more so that a person should spare his property: as regards ordinary people, that he should not squander it on ordinary people and not give all of it to others, but leave something for himself; [otherwise,] from what will he live?
rashi:a3.1: Gemara. “Of all that he has”: this is movable property, and not all movable property.
tosafot:a3.1: As the Sages taught: “Of all that he has,” and not all that he has: You might ask: this verse is written about a ḥerem given to the priests, since the end of the verse says “It shall not be sold or redeemed,” whereas dedications for Temple maintenance have redemption, like consecrated property. So how can the mishna say, “If for the Most High…”? This is not for the Most High but for the priests. Furthermore, in chapter HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 38b) it is taught: “Of man”: these are his Canaanite slaves and maidservants, and from this the Gemara challenges Rav, who said that one who consecrates his slave sets him free, because he meant that the slave should become one of the holy people. What is the challenge? Ḥeramim have no sanctity of the body, so they are not comparable to one who consecrates, of whom one can say he meant that the slave should become one of the holy people. One may answer that even ḥeramim given to the priests have sanctity of the body, as is taught later in this chapter (29a): Ḥeramim, so long as they are in the owner’s house, are like consecrated property in every respect; once he has given them to the priest, they are like non-sacred property in every respect. Evidently they have sanctity of the body.
rashi:a4.1: “Notwithstanding” [akh]: [the words] akh and rak are restrictions.
gershom:a4.1: The verse states “notwithstanding” [akh]: akh and rak are restrictions.
rashi:a6.1: By sharecropping [distoran]: he becomes a tenant farmer for others, taking fields for a half, a third or a quarter [of the crop].
gershom:a5.1: But a field: [I would have said] let him dedicate all his fields, for sharecropping is enough for him: he can take other people’s fields in tenancy and live from them.
gershom:a6.1: And had it taught us field alone, I would have said that this is why he may not dedicate all his fields, because his livelihood comes from them; but as for “of man,” say he may dedicate all his slaves, since a mere attendant is enough for him.
rashi:a6.2: But movable property, say he may dedicate all of it: [so] the Merciful One wrote “of all that he has,” and not all that he has, which is movable property.
gershom:a7.1: Because here and here there is livelihood: in both fields and slaves, for a person cannot live without a field and without slaves; and if he dedicates all his slaves, other good slaves are not always available to buy. But movable property, since other movables are available to buy whenever he wishes, say he may dedicate all of it. [So] the Merciful One wrote “of all that he has,” and not all.
gershom:a8.1: Just as an animal, which he has the right to sell outright, he may dedicate: to exclude his son and his daughter, his Hebrew slave and maidservant, and a purchased field, which he may not sell [outright].
rashi:a8.1: His daughter: he has the right to sell her while she is a minor, but not once she is a young woman [na’ara].
tosafot:a8.1: The verse states “animal”: just as an animal he has the right to sell forever: You might ask: if so, an ancestral field too [should be excluded], since if he sells it, it returns to the owner at the Jubilee. One may answer that in any case he has the right to remove it from his possession forever, for example if he consecrated it and another person redeemed it, so that it is divided among the priests at the Jubilee. Alternatively, one may answer that this is the meaning: just as he has the right to sell an animal, so too an ancestral field, as long as it is in his possession, he can sell; which is not so of his daughter, whom he has no right to sell once she has grown up.
gershom:a9.1: [Or, since he may sell his minor daughter, might he dedicate her? The verse states “animal”:] Just as an animal etc.: to exclude his daughter, whom he may sell only while she is a minor; once she has grown up he may no longer sell her.
gershom:a10.1: This is the first tanna: the first tanna also said that if he dedicated all of them, they are not dedicated.
rashi:a10.1: One who dispenses: to the poor.
rashi:a10.2: A fifth: for we learn it from Jacob, of whom two tenths are written [“I will surely give a tenth,” Genesis 28:22, doubles the word]. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya holds the view of Rabbi Ila, since he came to teach us that a person should spare his property. Rabbi Eliezer does not hold the view of Rabbi Ila: if one dispensed a great deal we are not concerned, so long as he left a little for himself, as with ḥerem.
gershom:a11.1: There is a difference between them regarding Rabbi Ila, who said in tractate Ketubot: One who dispenses his property to charity should not dispense more than a fifth, so that he will not come to need other people. The first tanna, who did not say “a person should spare,” does not hold Rabbi Ila’s view; rather, if he leaves a little for himself he may dedicate all the rest. And Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who said “a person should spare,” holds Rabbi Ila’s view, that he should spare [his property] and not dispense more than a fifth.
gershom:a12.1: Who sought to dispense more than a fifth.
gershom:a13.1: For a person may not dedicate an item that is not his: since his Hebrew slave and maidservant and a purchased field go out at the Jubilee.
gershom:a14.1: Priests and Levites may not dedicate: their property, for the law of ḥeramim does not apply to it, as is explained below.
rashi:a12.1: Mishna. For the dedications are theirs: as it is written, “Everything dedicated in Israel [shall be yours].” And since it is his, what is gained by it? If he dedicated it, he himself would acquire it and would not give it to another priest.
gershom:a15.1: For the dedications are theirs: what advantage is there? If he dedicated it, it would be his, since dedications go to the priests.
rashi:a13.1: The statement of Rabbi Yehuda appears correct: that Levites may not dedicate land.
gershom:a16.1: The statement of Rabbi Yehuda appears correct: who said that Levites may not dedicate land, as it is written, “For that is their perpetual possession.”
rashi:a13.2: And the statement of Rabbi Shimon with regard to movable property: since the dedications are not theirs. Therefore, if they dedicate movable property, the ḥerem takes effect on it and they give it to the priests.
gershom:a17.1: And the statement of Rabbi Shimon, who said that Levites may dedicate movable property: since the dedications are not theirs but the priests’, therefore they may dedicate.
gershom:a18.1: And movable property is juxtaposed to land: just as land may not be dedicated, so too movable property.
rashi:a14.1: Gemara. [From the latter clause:] since Rabbi needed to say “the statement of Rabbi Shimon appears correct with regard to movable property,” which implies that with regard to land his statement does not appear correct, by inference they disagree about land too.
gershom:a19.1: But from that which the latter clause teaches, “Rabbi said: The statement of Rabbi Yehuda appears correct with regard to land and the statement of Rabbi Shimon with regard to movable property”: Rabbi, who was deciding between them, says “appears”; but by inference Rabbi Shimon himself also says of land that Levites may dedicate it.
rashi:a16.1: For even Rabbi Shimon disagreed with him only etc.: and this is the meaning of Rabbi’s statement: the statement of Rabbi Yehuda appears correct to Rabbi Shimon with regard to land, for Rabbi Shimon’s statement concerns movable property.
gershom:a20.1: No; actually Rabbi Shimon holds that land may not be dedicated, and this is what it means: Rabbi says, the statement of Rabbi Yehuda appears correct to Rabbi Shimon, that Levites may not dedicate land, as it is written, “For that is their perpetual possession,” for even Rabbi Shimon disagreed with him only etc.
tosafot:a17.1: One who dedicated movable property gives it to any priest he wishes, as it is stated, “Everything dedicated in Israel shall be yours”: This is not the main derivation, since that verse is needed for what is expounded below (29a): Once he has given it to the priest it is like non-sacred property in every respect, as it is stated, “Everything dedicated in Israel shall be yours.” What is said here, that he gives them to any priest he wishes, is from reasoning, like teruma, which one gives to any priest and need not give to a priest of that watch. Furthermore, if it were the main derivation, what is the challenge below, “Let one juxtapose movable property to land”? It is a decree of the verse! Rather, learn from this that it is not the main derivation.
gershom:a21.1: One who dedicated movable property: it is speaking of an Israelite.
rashi:b1.1: Shall be yours: the Merciful One said this to Aaron, and all his descendants are included.
gershom:b1.1: As it is stated, “Everything dedicated in Israel shall be yours”: he gives them to whichever priest he wishes; that is, the benefit of choosing is his.
rashi:b2.1: The restitution for guilt that is made shall be the Lord’s, to the priest: the verse speaks of robbery from a convert, for among Israelites there is no one without kinsmen. Rather, one who robbed a convert, swore, admitted, and afterward [the convert] died, pays the principal and the fifth to the priest and [brings] a guilt offering for the altar. And we say in chapter HaGozel in Bava Kamma (110a): “The restitution for guilt”: this is the principal; “that is made”: this is the fifth; “besides the ram of atonement”: this is the ram of the guilt offering that he brings for the false oath he swore.
gershom:b2.1: As it is taught, “To the Lord, to the priest”: the verse speaks of robbery from a convert, for we expound the verse thus: “If the man has no kinsman”: this is a convert, who has no kinsmen.
rashi:b3.1: Here the verse speaks of a priest of that watch: for this is what the verse means: to the priest who atones for him with the ram of atonement shall the principal and the fifth belong.
gershom:b3.1: “Whereby atonement shall be made for him”: you must say that the verse speaks of a priest of that watch, who serves and sacrifices the offerings.
rashi:b4.1: A field that goes out etc.: Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin says it.
tosafot:b4.1: A field that goes out to the priests at the Jubilee is given to the watch on which the Jubilee fell: this statement is not from the baraita, but from the statement of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Avin [that] Rav Ḥisda said.
gershom:b4.1: He gives it to the watch on which the Jubilee fell: that the Jubilee began during its watch.
rashi:b4.2: It fell on: [that is,] the Jubilee [began] on Shabbat, when the watches change over, and Yom Kippur fell on it, on that very day: to which [watch] should he give it?
rashi:b4.3: To the outgoing watch: for the Jubilee began in its domain the previous evening.
gershom:b5.1: It fell on Shabbat: if the Jubilee began on Shabbat, and on Shabbat two watches serve, the outgoing watch and the incoming watch, to which watch does he give it? He gives it to the outgoing watch, since it is the one serving: it sacrificed the daily offerings last evening and this morning.
rashi:b5.1: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: It is taught in accordance with this: that we go by the beginning.
rashi:b5.2: You are found to say: since the forty-ninth year is the Sabbatical Year, and the year after it is the Jubilee.
rashi:b5.3: Both the Jubilee and the Sabbatical Year release at once: on one day, the Sabbatical Year releasing money loans and the Jubilee releasing sales of land, except that the Jubilee etc.
gershom:b6.1: Both the Jubilee and the Sabbatical Year release at once: that is, their releases meet one another, since the forty-ninth year is the Sabbatical Year and the fiftieth year is the Jubilee; except that the Jubilee releases at its beginning and the Sabbatical Year at its end.
rashi:b6.1: On the contrary: the reason that both release on one day is precisely that the Sabbatical Year [releases] at its end and the Jubilee at its beginning; for then it turns out that at twilight on the eve of the Jubilee the Sabbatical Year departs, and at that moment both release.
gershom:b7.1: On the contrary, it is because of this: that is, what is the reason they release at once? Because the Sabbatical Year releases money at its end and the Jubilee at its beginning. So instead of “except that,” correct it and teach: “because the Jubilee at its beginning etc.”
rashi:b7.1: Rather: teach it this way: they release at once because the Jubilee [releases] at its beginning and the Sabbatical Year at its end. [Rashi’s text of the Gemara reads “rather, teach” where ours reads “say.”]
gershom:b8.1: Granted, the Sabbatical Year releases at its end: this speaks of the release of money; for with regard to the release of land, as to sowing and plowing, they release from the beginning of the Sabbatical Year.
gershom:b9.1: As it is written: “At the end of every seven years you shall make a release,” and “This is the manner of the release…” [Deuteronomy 15:2].
gershom:b10.1: But the Jubilee at its beginning? The Jubilee takes effect on Yom Kippur. How, then, do they release at once? There are ten days between the end of the Sabbatical Year and the beginning of the Jubilee.
gershom:b11.1: Whose is this: [the teaching] that they release at once?
gershom:b12.1: It is Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka.
rashi:b7.2: [The view of] Rabbi Yishmael is in the first chapter of Rosh HaShana (8b).
rashi:b8.1: Ḥizkiyya bar Biluto heard it: this statement of Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin.
gershom:b13.1: Ḥizkiyya bar Biluto heard it: this that Ḥiyya bar Avin said.
rashi:b8.2: And let one juxtapose movable property: of ḥerem.
rashi:b8.3: To land: of ḥerem, since they are juxtaposed, as it is written, “of all that he has … or of his ancestral field”; so let us say that movable property too is given to a priest of that watch.
gershom:b14.1: He said it before Rabbi Abbahu: he said to him: Why did he say one gives them to any priest he wishes? Let one juxtapose movable property to land, so that one gives them to a priest of that watch.
rashi:b9.1: Is it not a dispute of tanna’im: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagreed about this above: Rabbi Yehuda juxtaposes and Rabbi Shimon does not juxtapose.
gershom:b15.1: Is it not a dispute of tanna’im: Rabbi Yehuda juxtaposes movable property to land and Rabbi Shimon does not juxtapose, and Rabbi Ḥiyya holds like the one who does not juxtapose.
tosafot:b9.1: In accordance with the one who does not juxtapose: You might ask about what we said above, “Granted, priests may not dedicate, as the dedications are theirs”: but dedicated fields must be given to a priest of that watch! If so, if a priest dedicated his field when it is not his watch, why need he not give it to a priest of that watch? One must say that this was said only to strengthen the point. For if a priest dedicated his field, it is no ḥerem, as it is written, “For that is their perpetual possession”; and although that is written about Levites, presumably the same holds for priests. And if a priest dedicated movable property, according to the one who juxtaposes it is obvious that he cannot dedicate it; and even according to the one who does not juxtapose, the dedications are theirs, as we said, since one gives them to any priest he wishes. This also settles what was said above, “And Rabbi Shimon: granted, priests, as we said”: he said it because of movable property, since although he does not juxtapose, the dedications are theirs in any case; but as for land, “perpetual possession,” written about Levites, applies equally to priests.
rashi:b10.1: Mishna. Dedications for priests: dedications that one dedicated in order to give them to the priest have no redemption, as it is written, “It shall not be sold or redeemed” (Leviticus 27:28). But dedications for Temple maintenance have redemption, for he dedicated them with this in mind, since only money is suitable for Temple maintenance.
tosafot:b10.1: Dedications for priests: that is, dedications given to the priests have no redemption, as it is written, “It shall not be sold or redeemed” (Leviticus 27:28). And [that verse] must be speaking of dedications for priests, even though it is written without specification, for if it were about dedications for Temple maintenance, it is obvious that they are redeemed, in order to use [the money] for the needs of Temple maintenance.
gershom:b16.1: Dedications for priests, which an Israelite dedicates intending that they reach a priest’s hand, have no redemption; rather, he gives them to the priests, as it is written, “Everything dedicated in Israel shall be yours.”
gershom:b17.1: Unspecified dedications: where he did not mention a priest.
rashi:b11.1: That it takes effect on offerings of the most sacred order etc.: as it explains: A person may dedicate his consecrated animals etc. And how are they dedicated? They are not his! Rather, if they are a vow, where he said, “It is incumbent upon me [to bring] a burnt offering,” and set aside an animal for his vow and afterward dedicated it: since he bears responsibility for it if it dies or is stolen, it turns out to be his, and he gives its full value to the priest and sacrifices the animal for his vow. For it certainly has redemption, since the animal itself was not dedicated, as it is not his.
gershom:b18.1: That it takes effect on offerings of the most sacred order and offerings of lesser sanctity: how? As it explains below. Not that he can attach the offerings themselves to some ḥerem or anything else, for consecration does not take effect on consecrated items; rather, as it explains: A person may dedicate his consecrated animals, whether offerings of the most sacred order or offerings of lesser sanctity. If they are a vow, where he said “incumbent upon me,” so that he is responsible for it, he gives their value to the priests because he dedicated them, and the animals themselves are not [treated] as ḥerem but are sacrificed for his obligation. And if they are a gift offering, for which he is not responsible, they do not count as his property, and he gives the priests on account of the ḥerem only its benefit, the monetary benefit he is permitted to take from it. And it explains how he gives its benefit: he said, “This bull is a burnt offering,” not saying “incumbent upon me,” so that he is not responsible for it, and afterward he said, “It is ḥerem”: one estimates how much a person etc. Even though it is a gift offering and he is not responsible for it, still, a person who is not obligated to bring a burnt offering would buy one if he found it cheaply, and that responsibility would be upon him; and he gives that sum. Another explanation: one estimates how much a person, a priest who is not of the watch now serving, would want to give the donor for this bull so that he would wait for him and give it to him to sacrifice as a burnt offering during his own watch, so that he would acquire its hide. As much as that priest would give him, so much this one who dedicated it gives the priests. And this is [the case of] offerings of the most sacred order.
rashi:b13.1: And if it is a gift offering: where he is not responsible for it if it dies, certainly the ḥerem does not take effect [on the animal’s value], since it is not his.
rashi:b13.2: Rather, by its benefit: the monetary benefit he has in it he gives to the priest. How? [He said,] “This bull is a burnt offering,” and dedicated it: one estimates how much a person would want to give for this bull to sacrifice it as a burnt offering that he is not obligated [to bring]. That is to say, a person who is not obligated to bring a burnt offering, if he finds one cheaply, takes it to sacrifice as a gift to his Maker; and this man gives that sum. For this is the monetary benefit he has in it: if it died or was stolen he is not responsible for it, since once he set it aside he fulfilled his obligation, and from then on, if it is lost, he loses only that he has not sacrificed a gift to his Maker. So what he has lost is the offering of a burnt offering that he is not obligated [to bring]. Some books read, “to sacrifice a burnt offering that he is not permitted,” and it is the same thing.
rashi:b13.3: Permitted [rashai]: a term meaning obligated, [as] “a creditor” [noshe] (Exodus 22:24) is rendered in the Targum rashya.
tosafot:b13.1: One estimates how much a person would want to give for this bull to sacrifice it as a burnt offering, even though he is not rashai: that is, he is not obligated, as noshe [a creditor] is rendered in the Targum rashya; so Rashi explained. Accordingly, the master Rabbi Ya’akov bar Shimshon says that what is taught in the first chapter of Kiddushin (33a), “Craftsmen are not rashain to stand before Torah scholars while they are engaged in their work,” applies even when they are engaged in their own work, and rashain means “obligated,” like “even though he is not rashai” here, which means “even though he is not obligated.” And if it speaks of work for others, one may well read rashain in its plain sense [“permitted”].
gershom:b19.1: [The printed text here is corrupt; an editor’s note proposes the reading:] Even though he is not rashai: that is, he is not obligated at all to sacrifice a burnt offering; that is, since he is not responsible for it, he does not give its full value, only its monetary benefit, as we said.
gershom:b20.1: And offerings of lesser sanctity, how? A firstborn, while it is in an Israelite’s possession, whether unblemished or blemished, may be dedicated, [and he gives] its monetary benefit and not its full value, since he is not responsible for it. And how does one redeem it? That is, how does one assess its benefit? One estimates how much an Israelite would want to give the owner for this firstborn so that he would give it to his daughter’s son who is a priest, or to his sister’s son who is a priest; so much this one who dedicated it gives the priests.
rashi:b14.1: And how does one redeem it: for the firstborn itself is not dedicated, since it is not his but the priest’s.
rashi:b14.2: Rather, one estimates how much a person, an Israelite, would want to give this householder so that he gives his firstborn to his daughter’s son who is a priest, or to his sister’s son; and that monetary benefit this householder gives to the priest on account of the ḥerem. It says specifically a daughter’s son and a sister’s son who are priests, because then the one who gives him that benefit is an Israelite. But with a son’s son who is a priest, or a brother’s son who is a priest, the one who would give him that benefit is a priest, and he may not pay a fee for it: even though he is not giving for his own sake, since the firstborn is fit for him too, he looks like a priest who helps at the threshing floors, threshing and winnowing, so that they will give him their teruma as his wage, and it turns out that he takes it not as teruma but as a wage. And so we say in Bekhorot, in chapter Ad Kamma (Bekhorot 26b).
tosafot:b14.1: To his daughter’s son or his sister’s son who is a priest: one cannot say his son’s son or his brother’s son, because since [the firstborn] is fit for him, he is like a priest who helps at the threshing floors, as is found in chapter Ad Kamma (Bekhorot 26b). And so Rashi explained.
